articles.title: This TP-Link router automatically moves its antenna for the best Wi-Fi
articles.summary: The TP-Link Archer AXE200 Omni router automatically seeks out the best possible signal and adjusts its antennas for optimal reception.
articles.body: In what is likely one of the stranger innovations at CES this year, TP-Link is showing off the prototype for its new Archer AXE200 Omni router. There are plenty of new routers taking advantage of 6E connectivity debuting at this year’s CES, but the engineering of this particular router is sure to raise some eyebrows. [Image: The AXE200 features four antennas that automatically fold out and rotate to seek out the best possible signal, wherever it happens to be. While the necessity of this particular feature is debatable, it’s pretty wild to see a router come to life and instinctively articulate its arms like some kind of alien homing beacon. [Image: While the effectiveness of this particular feature isn’t certain, the technical specs are definitely impressive. As you might expect from a 6E router, the AXE200 features improved tri-band speed, with a 6Ghz band joining the existing 5Ghz and 2.4Ghz bands. Additionally, the Wi-Fi 6E compatibility allows the router to exploit additional bandwidth and reduce latency overall. The AXE200 is still in the prototype stages, so there isn’t any information regarding the price point or a release window. For anyone in the market for something a little more conventional, TP-Link is also premiering its Archer AXE300 quad-band router, which doesn’t feature autonomous antennas but shares the same extraterrestrial design. The AXE300 takes full advantage of WiFi 6E with duplicate 5GHz bands in addition to the 6Ghz and 2.4Ghz bands. The price for this particular unit is to be determined but is scheduled to become available in Q2 of 2022.

articles.title: Instagram head Adam Mosseri explains what makes iPhone Duo ‘a bit of a tricky form factor’ for Instagram
articles.summary: Instagram head Adam Mosseri has admitted that getting the app right on Apple’s iPhone Duo is harder than it looks.
articles.body: Instagram head Adam Mosseri has admitted that getting the app right on Apple’s iPhone Duo is harder than it looks. Replying to users on Threads, Mosseri said it will be “pretty challenging” to make Instagram feel great on the foldable, calling it “a bit of a tricky form factor”. The remarks stand out because Instagram is one of the apps Apple itself has tagged as “Made for iPhone Duo”.In a separate post, Mosseri pointed to a specific clash. When the Duo is closed, Apple places navigation buttons along the right-hand edge of the screen. That is exactly where Instagram keeps the like, comment and share buttons on Reels, so two sets of controls end up competing for the same strip of display.iPhone Duo’s side-mounted controls are forcing apps like Instagram to rethink their layoutThe Duo is Apple’s first foldable, and its interface shifts many controls to the right edge instead of the bottom. Apps built for tall 20:9 screens don’t always adapt neatly. On the unfolded display, early users found Instagram sitting in the middle with empty space on either side. Rotating the phone pushed controls back to the bottom, the back button jumped to the top-left corner, and Stories didn’t fill the screen.Instagram’s iPhone Duo update puts Reels and comments side by sideInstagram has now rolled out a dedicated iPhone Duo version of its app. With the phone open, the main feed stretches into a wider layout, and Reels play at full size with comments alongside, so the video keeps running while you read. Control buttons now sit in a sidebar. Messages and notifications open in two columns, with the inbox on one side and the chat on the other.The wider app catalogue is moving quickly too. Apple’s marketing chief Greg Joswiak said on November 16 that more than 200,000 apps are now optimised for the iPhone Duo, double the 100,000 figure Apple shared earlier this month. The count covers apps built with the iOS 27.1 SDK or later that fill both displays and use vertical controls in the status bar.Instagram’s update, though, mostly reworks the unfolded screen. On the closed phone, Stories and Reels keep their familiar vertical format, and that is where Mosseri spotted the button clash in the first place.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Windows 11 actually runs better on 8GB of RAM now
articles.summary: I retested the base Surface Laptop, and Microsoft’s optimizations seem to be working.
articles.body: As recently as the beginning of the year, 16GB of RAM was common on sub-$800 Windows laptops, which helped compensate for an increasingly bloated-feeling Windows 11. But with the cost of RAM skyrocketing this year, 8GB is once again typical for a starting configuration. The MacBook Neo got away with it, but Windows laptops, including Microsoft’s own 13-inch Surface Laptop, could struggle. Microsoft was talking a big game about making Windows faster and more reliable before the RAM crisis really hit, and it now seems like that effort is beginning to bear fruit. Earlier this month, Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft’s EVP of Windows and devices, detailed in a blog post the improvements the company has made to Windows 11 to address the constraints of 8GB PCs. In it, Davuluri claims, “Windows is now up to 20% more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40% faster in our lab test.” The most significant change is in memory management. When there isn’t enough available memory to handle all active data, some of it has to be offloaded (or “paged out”) to storage. And SSDs, especially in lower-cost laptops, are much slower than RAM. [Image: Windows 11 consistently takes up most of the available RAM on an 8GB system, even when idle. But it manages it better now. When Windows needs to access data that’s been paged out from the RAM to the SSD, it’s called a hard fault (or page fault). If it happens a lot — say, on a laptop with only 8GB of RAM — it leads to little slowdowns like browser tabs requiring a refresh before you can access them again. Davuluri says, “Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return.” To test this, I fired up the same 13-inch Surface Laptop with 8GB of RAM that I reviewed back in July, when I proclaimed eight is not enough for Windows. This laptop was one of the worst examples of RAMageddon’s current stranglehold on computing: With half the RAM of last year’s base model, it struggled to keep up with my regular workload. And this is Microsoft’s hardware. Before updating the Surface to the latest Windows 11 build, I got reacquainted with this laptop and the version of Windows I left it on (25H2, build 26200.8875). It was rough. Running about 20 tabs (on the latest Chrome build) while streaming a 4K YouTube video and using Slack and Signal made everything from clicking tabs to swiping around Windows with trackpad gestures feel sluggish. Chrome tabs and apps would refresh after leaving them in the background for just a short moment. When you’re multitasking and bouncing between many tabs, like when researching something, those refreshes get incredibly frustrating. And the fan was running audibly the whole time. Keeping the Resource Monitor open showed memory hard faults ranging from just under 700 faults per second to 29,000 faults per second, during which Windows ground to a halt. Seeing this number literally go off its chart showed just how badly Windows 11 struggled with memory management on 8GB before the update. [Image: Before running recent Windows updates, the 8GB Surface Laptop could sometimes seize under load with many hard faults per second. Now, after updating the Surface Laptop to Windows 11 version 26H2, build 26300.9974 (memory improvements are live on build 26300.9818 and beyond) things are much improved. I opened over 30 Chrome tabs while streaming the same 4K YouTube video and running the same chat apps, and Windows slowed a bit, but nowhere near as much. I could feel things like Task View get a little less responsive and at times stuttery, but it was the way you’d expect when taxing a system. Chrome tabs required less frequent refreshes. The fan also took longer to kick in and ran a little quieter and for shorter durations when it did. Taking a fresh look at the Resource Monitor, hard faults at normal operation were now under 300 per second, with occasional jumps to about 1,000. Performance was even slightly better when I subbed out Chrome for Microsoft Edge. Edge felt more responsive under load and had fewer hard faults when running 30 tabs, the same 4K YouTube video, and a Google Meet video call. [Image: [Image: I’m happy to see that the 8GB Surface Laptop now performs better, and I’m equally relieved that Windows 11 is starting to feel more viable on 8GB of RAM. (It’s still a shame the 8GB Surface Laptop costs more than last year’s 16GB, but I digress.) Do I want 8GB of RAM in any laptop I’m personally buying? No. As I said when I reviewed the latest Dell XPS 13, I appreciate that 8GB is workable — and it should be fine for basic needs today — but I still advise getting 16GB if you’re able. The extra headroom will keep things speedy for longer, especially after you bog a computer down with lots of files, apps, or games. And as much better as the 8GB Surface Laptop is now, I still managed to crash Chrome entirely with fewer than three dozen tabs. Microsoft has done better by its entry-level laptop, but it’s not a miracle worker. Our ongoing RAMageddon makes living with lower quantities of memory a grim reality. Microsoft is partly to blame for that, of course. And it hasn’t done itself any favors with all the feature bloat it put into Windows 11 during the Copilot / AI era. Meanwhile, other OSes, like Linux, macOS, and ChromeOS, can get by better with less. Still, I’m glad to see Microsoft ever so slightly right the ship in this one way. Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

articles.title: Get ready for a nationwide emergency alert test at 2:20PM ET today
articles.summary: FEMA and the FCC will interrupt radio and TV programming to test the nationwide Emergency Alert System.
articles.body: Radio and TV broadcasts will be interrupted for about one minute at 2:20PM ET today while FEMA and the FCC test the country’s Emergency Alert System. Unlike recent communications outages, this is a planned interruption that FEMA is required to run every three years. FEMA says today’s test includes radio and television broadcasters, cable systems, satellite radio and television providers, and wireline video providers. This test doesn’t include phones. You’ll hear high-pitched alert tones and the following test message: > This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. This is only a test. No action is required by the public. Radio and TV programming will continue as usual after the test wraps up. FEMA runs tests like this when there’s not an actual emergency so it can find technical and operational issues with the Emergency Alert System. If there is a real emergency or severe weather event today, the test will run on December 3rd instead.

articles.title: This E Ink photo frame can double as your family’s digital dashboard
articles.summary: Trmnl’s new Frame uses a large Spectra 6 color E Ink screen to display photos, paintings, artwork, or even your family’s calendar.
articles.body: Trmnl, a company best known for its highly customizable E Ink dashboards that can function as anything from a desktop calendar to a stock tracker, has introduced a new display that’s also well suited for showing artwork and photos. It’s not the company’s first color E Ink device, but instead of being limited to just four colors, the new Frame can display thousands of shades using a 31.5-inch E Ink Spectra 6 panel, similar to what you’ll find in products from Aura and Pocketbook. The Frame is now available for preorder for $1,299 in a handmade wooden body and you can choose from four different types of wood: white oak, cherry, sapele, and walnut. The first batch will be a limited run of around 470 units that’s already more than half sold out, and delivery of most of the displays is expected to happen in early 2027. Optional add-ons include a matching wooden kickstand if you don’t want to hang it on a wall, and a larger 20,000mAh battery. However, the Frame should run for months between charges with the standard 10,000mAh option. [Product: Trmnl Frame | What sets the Frame apart from other large format E Ink art frames and posters is that it’s open source and can do more than display images. Through plugins you can build yourself, or download from a marketplace featuring over 1,400 at this point, the Frame can also be used as a dashboard showing the weather, to-do lists, or whatever info you want hanging on your wall. [Media: If you do use it for displaying imagery, Trmnl developed Lazarus, a color conversion engine the company believes provides the “best color matching on the market for any Spectra 6 display.” If you disagree, because the Frame is open source, you can adjust the color tuning to match your own preferences. As with Trmnl’s other E Ink products, the Frame can be connected to the internet to dynamically display whatever information you need it to. But to further extend its battery life, you can also fill a microSD card with a folder of images files and use the Frame offline. You can customize how frequently a new photo is displayed, or set up schedules so that your favorite piece of art stays on screen longer than others. While the Frame is more expensive than other E Ink Spectra 6 products currently available, the appeal here is the flexibility to use it as more than just a digital poster.

articles.title: You can now preorder the Flipper One that puts a Linux computer in your pocket
articles.summary: After announcing it several months ago, the Flipper One is launching through a Kickstarter campaign where you can preorder it for $399 ahead of a 2027 release.
articles.body: After first announcing its Flipper One last May, which the company describes as an “open Linux multi-tool built for high-performance computing and IP networking,” Flipper Devices has launched a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign where you can preorder the device for $399 with shipping expected to start in July 2027. The Flipper One is more expensive than the company’s popular but controversial Flipper Zero wireless hacking multitool, which is currently available for $169. However, Flipper Devices points out that the new Flipper One isn’t a successor to the Flipper Zero, but a completely different product. While the Zero’s capabilities focused on NFC, RFID, infrared, and Sub-1GHz wireless frequencies, the much larger Flipper One offers expanded connectivity with two gigabit ethernet ports, PCIe, SATA, and USB 3.0 interfaces, and Wi-Fi 6e support. There’s also an M.2 slot for connecting modules that include a 5G modem and a mesh networking LoRa radio that can turn the Flipper One into a walkie-talkie. [Image: The Flipper One can be used as a network diagnostic tool using its built-in ethernet ports, or you can connect it to a TV over USB-C or HDMI and use it as a tiny media player. It’s still pocket-friendly, but the Flipper One is powered by an 8-core RK3576 ARM processor with a dedicated NPU and a GPU that supports connectivity to an external display over USB-C or HDMI. Flipper Devices suggests the One can be used as everything from a networking diagnostics tool to a media player when connected to a TV. It runs Flipper OS, which is based on Debian Linux and features an open source firmware so that users can develop their own apps, tools, and uses for the device. [Image: While the Flipper Zero focused on wireless technologies like NFC and RFID, the larger Flipper One includes many interface ports and connectors.

articles.title: 'No one could tell them no': Jensen Huang's daughter Madison, son-in-law played big role in Nvidia's response to Megaspeed probe - report
articles.summary: Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison Huang, played a significant role in managing the company's public response to scrutiny over
articles.body: Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison Huang, played a significant role in managing the company's public response to scrutiny over its business relationship with Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed, which is at the centre of a US investigation into the alleged diversion of advanced chips to China, according to a Financial Times report.Madison Huang, a senior director of product marketing at Nvidia, took on responsibilities beyond her formal role, helping direct the company's response to growing media scrutiny of Megaspeed, three people familiar with the matter told the Financial Times.Her involvement, along with the role played by her husband and fellow Nvidia executive Nico Caprez, is expected to attract greater scrutiny as the company's board investigates the circumstances surrounding its relationship with Megaspeed.The developments come days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO following reports of alleged relationships with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who US intelligence officials suspect of having links to Chinese espionage efforts, and a subordinate at Nvidia.Madison Huang took charge of communications responseAccording to the Financial Times, Madison Huang began involving herself directly in Nvidia's communications strategy in autumn 2025, when the company's dealings with Megaspeed started attracting media attention.She had privately hired crisis public relations firm Heller for the Huang family in spring 2025. The firm, known for handling high-profile individuals involved in sexual misconduct controversies, later began working directly for Nvidia.Around the same time, Madison Huang temporarily excluded one of Nvidia's senior corporate communications executives from the internal group discussing how to respond to questions about the company's chip sales to Megaspeed. The group that remained involved in preparing responses included Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter.One Nvidia colleague described the influence exercised by Madison Huang and Caprez within the company, telling the Financial Times, “They had a lot of power and influence and were allowed to operate unchecked. No one could tell them ‘no’ or put them in their place," as cited by the Financial Times.The report also raised questions about the company's governance, with current and former employees expressing concerns over Jensen Huang's decision to place family members in senior positions at Nvidia, even before his departure.Caprez's growing role in Nvidia's Asia businessCaprez, whom Madison Huang recently married, also assumed a broader role in Nvidia's international business as scrutiny of Megaspeed intensified.A fellow Nvidia executive, Caprez joined the company in 2024 and was promoted in autumn 2025 to a director-level position overseeing its international cloud computing partnerships in Asia.Two people familiar with the matter told the Financial Times that Caprez had travelled to Asia to oversee deals with cloud providers and had been involved in transactions with regional cloud partners months before his formal promotion. Megaspeed was among Nvidia's largest customers in Southeast Asia.By January 2026, Caprez had been promoted again to vice-president of global AI infrastructure growth.A Swiss national and former professional skier and consultant, Caprez met Madison Huang while both were studying at London Business School.The links of both executives to Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed are expected to face greater scrutiny as the company's board conducts an investigation led by a former senior US prosecutor.US investigation into Megaspeed and alleged chip diversionMegaspeed has been under US investigation since 2024 over suspicions that it was involved in diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of American export controls. The Singapore-based company purchased approximately $5 billion worth of Nvidia hardware.According to information released by the US Commerce and Justice departments on Monday, the investigation began after authorities detected suspicious activity involving the possible diversion of sensitive semiconductors.The US Commerce Department approached Nvidia in May 2025 seeking records of its direct and indirect sales to Megaspeed. The chipmaker placed the Singapore company on its restricted sales list the following month.The two departments said in a joint statement, "After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the department of commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations."In June 2025, US agents travelled to Megaspeed's premises alongside Singaporean law enforcement officials to conduct an "on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed". They also questioned Alice Huang, who was then the company's chief executive.The Justice Department subsequently took charge of the criminal investigation. The agencies said they were making details of the case public despite the usual practice of not commenting on ongoing investigations, citing public interest.Nvidia had earlier told the New York Times that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities several times, found no Chinese shareholders and detected no evidence of chip smuggling.The company has also maintained that it placed Megaspeed on its "block list" in June 2025, "prohibiting any further sales or shipments".Nvidia, representatives for the Huang family and Heller declined to comment on the latest allegations.Jensen Huang summoned to testify before US CongressThe controversy has also drawn congressional attention, with Jensen Huang summoned to testify about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed at a closed-door session in December.The former CEO has agreed to appear before the House committees on Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China for transcribed interviews on December 1. Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter is expected to appear before the committees on December 2.The committee chairs, Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, said in a joint statement on Tuesday, “We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security.”Meanwhile, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has criticised Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his department for failing to place Megaspeed on the US blacklist. The Commerce Department has delayed new additions to the list.On Tuesday, Nvidia's board also established a new National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to supervise the company's compliance with US national security and export regulations.Alice Huang faces scrutiny in SingaporeMegaspeed's former executive Alice Huang has also come under scrutiny over suspected links to Chinese espionage efforts. US intelligence officials reportedly believe she had a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, an allegation that, along with reports of a second relationship involving a subordinate, preceded his resignation on November 12 after 33 years at the helm of Nvidia.Megaspeed said on Sunday that Alice Huang had formally left the company on August 30, 2025, while maintaining that it had conducted a "legitimate and lawful business."Singapore's government said last week that Alice Huang had previously held three key positions at Megaspeed: chief executive, chairperson and one of its key controllers.Singapore police found insufficient evidence to establish that she had committed offences related to suspected false declarations over server purchases. However, authorities issued her a warning for knowingly providing inaccurate information that downplayed her role in the company.Singapore has also barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country, while investigations involving Megaspeed and six other individuals remain underway, according to the Home Affairs Ministry.The Singapore government said on Monday that it had agreed to continue discussions with Washington over the company.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: Jon Stewart on Trump administration response to air travel crisis: ‘So chaotic and amateurish’
articles.summary: Late-night hosts discussed the administration’s unhelpful response to the FAA’s rare ground stop this weekend
articles.body:
Late-night hosts responded to the FAA's sudden, rare ground stop as Donald Trump shirks any responsibility for the transportation crisis.

Jon Stewart opened Monday's Daily Show with a recap of the Federal Aviation Administration's shock ground stoppage on Friday afternoon, which stranded travelers across the country and led to cascading delays. Stewart had particular ire for the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, who comforted worried travelers on Friday evening with: "This isn't another 9/11."

"Who said 9/11! Why would you bring up 9/11?!" Stewart marveled. "These motherfuckers just want to know if they're going to miss their connecting flights!"

Later in his press conference, as the crisis was still unfolding, Mullin took the time to correct a reporter who asked if the stoppage was related to an AI error – "We call it SI [super intelligence] around here, remember?" he said.

"That's your problem?" Stewart mocked. "Deadnaming the robots? You just invoked 9/11, and now you're the grammar police? 'Uh, excuse me, miss, the planes will be crashing into the Gulf of America .'

"This is so chaotic and amateurish – which makes sense," he added. As Mullin said, "This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like."

And "while it may feel like all of our nation's critical systems are falling apart, each one on a different day, like an advent calendar of societal collapse, help is on the way," Stewart added, referring to the rumored comeback of the disgraced Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, following his affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

"A comeback? Oh, it's been a long weekend," Stewart quipped. "What'd you do, one day of soul-searching per affair? A comeback? How is this even possible?" Stewart then cut to a clip of Trump saying that he "would not mind" Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia because "he's a great, brilliant person, and we want to protect our brilliant people."

"The entire Jensen Huang soap opera exposes how all of these tech titans have us normies by the short and curlies," said Stewart. "Like they're creating the most powerful technology that the world has ever seen. Even they say in their filing to go public could pose an existential threat to humanity, but we are not even allowed to regulate them."

"Sometimes it feels like maybe Elon and his Doge bros shouldn't have fired more than a thousand employees at the FAA," said Jimmy Kimmel on Monday evening, as US air travel still faced numerous delays and cancellations.

"We learned this weekend a very valuable lesson: we learned what happens when the only experience your secretary of transportation has when it comes to transportation is being on Road Rules All Stars on MTV.

"And where, you may ask, was the president during all of this?" Kimmel continued. "He was in the Oval Office meeting with his 87-year-old ambassador to Hollywood, Jon Voight. Trump pulled a real disappearing act on this one. He didn't post about it Friday or Saturday. But he did find time to complain about the public golf course he's trying to forcibly renovate in Washington."

That would be the city's East Potomac Park and Golf Link, which Trump calls "Trash Island". Trump wrote on Truth Social: "Trash Island is currently the worst golf course anywhere in the world. The fairways are far too close together. When you walk down the corridors of Trash Island, you don't hear the sound of the running Potomac. All you hear is the sound of people screaming, 'FORE!'"

"You might be wondering, with all that's going on, why the president is posting about 'Trash Island'," Kimmel noted. "It's very simple: Now that he can't go to Epstein's island, you know, he needs an island. He needs one island at all times."

And on Late Night, Seth Meyers skewered Trump's refusal to engage with the FAA stoppage on any level. As Trump told the press on Monday: "I don't take any responsibility."

"No, of course not! Why would you?" Meyers retorted. "The constitution says the president's only responsibilities are tweets, memes and ballrooms.

"After several days of near silence, the president finally emerged from hiding to explain to a worried nation that the air traffic control system, the one that keeps us all safe while flying, had a heart attack and that's why he wants to blow it up," said Meyers of Trump's eventual comments on the matter to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House. "Is there anything else you'd like to explain to the class before we go to the school board and demand to have you removed?"

Meyers then played a clip of Trump claiming that "the Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass" for the nation's flight communication system, which was not advised "if you know anything about electrical engineering".

"Now, if you're wondering if you cannot hook up copper into glass, the answer is actually yes, he's correct," Meyers joked.

"Of course he's not fucking right!" he added. "You can transmit data from copper to glass the same way Trump transmits data to the media from his ass. Do you seriously think the same oatmeal-brained 80-year-old who once spelled the word tap with two Ps was secretly an electrical engineer this whole time?"

articles.title: Inside Microsoft’s giant Outlook outage
articles.summary: A bug took down Microsoft’s email services for millions around the world.
articles.body: At 9AM last Thursday, everything seemed normal. Microsoft employees were arriving on campus, ready for a regular day of emails and meetings. But barely an hour later, one of Microsoft’s worst outages in history started to unfold, leaving employees, businesses, and many governments without access to Outlook emails for nearly 24 hours. It all started in Switzerland, according to a source familiar with the outage. Exchange Online servers that power Outlook started to fall offline. The problem quickly spread to Mexico, and then to other countries around the world, as Microsoft’s failover systems tried to shift email traffic elsewhere. Within a couple of hours, more than 80 percent of Exchange servers were unresponsive. Sources tell me that Microsoft marked the outage as “sev0” in its internal incident tracking system, the highest level, which indicates a catastrophic level of service disruption. Hundreds of engineers began trying to figure out what had gone wrong, and how to restore service. It’s not unusual for servers to fail under certain circumstances, but Microsoft has a variety of systems that are supposed to route traffic toward healthy servers to keep the broader system online. In this case, the failover systems did their job, but they also spread the problem. In the early hours of the outage, engineers were analyzing crash reports, trace logs, and kernel dumps to try and find clues to the giant outage. Some servers had entered into maintenance mode and became unresponsive due to unusually high CPU loads. Engineers tried to bring servers back online, but they were almost immediately overwhelmed by traffic waiting to access the servers. Exchange servers boot up and run an OS over a network (Preboot Execution Environment), a process that allows Microsoft’s support staff and engineers to manage OS updates remotely. I understand that the sudden burst of traffic from servers being rebooted was overwhelming the systems monitoring them, causing a form of reboot loop where they kept trying and failing to come back online. As engineers continued to hunt for the root cause, Microsoft was even struggling to roll back servers to a healthy state using its usual processes of reverting recent changes. As the outside world began to wonder if this outage was related to a cyberattack or sloppy AI coding, Microsoft’s engineers were already investigating potential attack vectors and liaising with DDoS specialists to understand whether this could have been an attack. I’m told crash reports and logs quickly ruled out the possibility of an attack, and after recent rollbacks failed, Microsoft’s engineers began to take a closer look at the networking stack of the servers and discovered an unusual bug. It was unusual because the bug had been sitting on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers since July without any impact to servers. “A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions,” wrote Charles Lamanna, the leader of Microsoft’s Copilot, Agents, and Platform (CAP) team, in a post on X. The teams behind Office, Outlook, and Microsoft Teams all started reporting to Lamanna last month after the head of Office and Teams, Ryan Roslansky, left the company. Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report describes the bug as one affecting select Windows servers “due to lock contention inside an internal Windows process.” The bug doesn’t affect regular versions of Windows since it was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Microsoft didn’t find the bug until this major outage, and it admits that was because of the traffic mix and hardware used in its testing labs. “The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores,” Lamanna wrote. The bug became obvious because of two other incidents that increased load and reduced server capacity. Fifteen hours before this Outlook outage began, Microsoft Teams failed over from an alternative networking gateway to the main gateway that supports Exchange Online. “This increased the load on the networking gateway and changed its traffic patterns,” Lamanna wrote. Ordinarily this wouldn’t have been a problem, but at the same time around 14 percent of server capacity for this gateway was “out of service due to an unrelated issue from the previous day.” The trifecta of a bug, Microsoft Teams failing over, and reduced server capacity all caused the network gateway to trigger the problem that had been lying dormant since July. It took Microsoft nearly 24 hours to get its Exchange servers stable again, and I’m told overlapping interventions from teams trying to fix issues complicated coordination at times. Microsoft engineers had a running bridge call the entire time, and at one point it hit the maximum of 1,000 participants. That shows you how many teams were involved with trying to find the root cause of this huge outage, which started at the peak window of traffic in the US. “Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again,” Lamanna wrote. “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state. Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change.” Microsoft is now working on a final post-incident review that will be published later this week. Even without that full review, it’s clear that the company will need to invest more into its testing processes to ensure that when something like this happens again, it can catch the problem a lot sooner. Outages happen daily, but this kind of cascading failure is a rare moment for Microsoft to learn from its mistakes and make sure the same sequence of events doesn’t bring down Outlook for millions of people again. Notepad will return in December after next week’s Thanksgiving break. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there. Thanks for subscribing to Notepad.

articles.title: The iPhone Duo feels far more intuitive with Apple’s new face unlock
articles.summary: There are limitations compared with Face ID, but this is much better than nothing.
articles.body: Apple is testing adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — not true Face ID, but something a little simpler and less secure. So far, it works great, and even with a few Apple-imposed security limitations, it makes the Duo quicker and more comfortable to use than relying on Touch ID every time. That’s one of my gripes with the phone taken care of. The Duo’s foldable architecture means that Apple couldn’t fit in the full Face ID sensor array found on the rest of the iPhone lineup (though it reportedly hopes to change that by the second generation). Instead, it simply has two selfie cameras — one on the outer display, and another hidden under the inner one. Neither supports full Face ID, but after enough grumbling from reviewers and early adopters that using Touch ID alone feels cumbersome, Apple has relented. The latest developer beta of iOS 27.3 introduces a new option to “Unlock with Front Camera” — Apple is careful not to call it Face ID. Setup is similar, though instead of rotating your head in a slow circle, you simply have to turn it left, right, up, and down. It takes five seconds or so, and I even managed it under the jerky conditions of a moving London bus. [Image: Setup takes only a few seconds and is similar to Face ID. The new face unlock brings convenience, taking just half a second to unlock, but Apple warns during setup that it “isn’t as secure as Touch ID or Face ID” because it lacks the infrared depth map of the TrueDepth cameras. That means it’s possible to spoof with a photograph or video clip, but I managed that only once in over 20 attempts. Crucially, after each failed attempt to trick the system with a photo, the phone demanded I use Touch ID for my next login — which it doesn’t require if it simply doesn’t detect any face in the frame. That means getting past this would require any would-be thief or spy to get the fake face right the first time. Lacking TrueDepth also introduces limits in low light, though performance is better than I expected. Walking around after sunset, I had to seek out especially dark spots before I could find anywhere where unlocking failed, like huddling behind a truck on a leafy street where the streetlights couldn’t reach me. It will fail eventually, but it does have to get quite dark for that to happen. Apple has imposed a few other limitations to reflect the lower security of the new system. You can only use it to unlock the phone from the lockscreen, so you will have to revert to Touch ID or a passcode to use Apple Pay, install or log in to an app, or get past any other screen where the phone requires security credentials. That’s similar to most Android phones with camera-based face unlock. Only Google’s Pixel phones allow you to make purchases or log in to apps using Face Unlock, thanks to software tricks that make the system more secure than other Android alternatives, Google says. [Image: [Image: The iPhone Duo’s more annoying limitations reflect when you can use the feature. Face unlock works only for 45 minutes at a time, after which you’ll have to verify with Touch ID or your passcode the next time you unlock. Worse, it doesn’t work at all with the inner screen’s under-display selfie camera. Apple hasn’t said why, though presumably it felt the lower resolution and quality of that camera made face unlock unsuitable. I’d love it if Apple loosened its restrictions just a little — 45 minutes isn’t a very long time before requiring Touch ID again, and I’m sure I’ll regularly forget that the inner screen requires a fingerprint. But the Duo already feels more comfortable to use, letting me get straight into the phone rather than fumbling for the fingerprint sensor. It’s small, but it’s a welcome sign that Apple is listening to the Duo’s early users and is willing to adjust its grand vision to meet the world where it is. For now, face unlock is limited to the developer beta, but it could roll out to a public beta within a few days, and with luck will get a full launch along with the rest of iOS 27.3 in December. Now can we get the same option for MacBooks and iPads? Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: Amflow’s new urban e-bike series is deliciously overpowered for flat city streets
articles.summary: DJI-backed e-bike brand Amflow has announced its first urban commuter bikes, the UE Carbon ($3,500) and UE Carbon Pro ($3,900), featuring a 1,100W Avinox M2 motor, 82-mile range, wireless charging, and Apple’s Find My tracker.
articles.body: DJI spinoff Amflow has spent the last couple of years shaking up the electric mountain bike (eMTB) market with ridiculously high-torque, lightweight models. Today, it’s bringing that same overengineered energy to pavement with the UE Series, its first urban commuter line. The series consists of two models: the UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro. Both pack 125Nm of torque, 1,100W of peak power, and an 8x max assist ratio capable of climbing 30 percent grades — all while operating quietly under 45dBA (quieter than a household refrigerator). A swappable 600Wh battery provides up to 132km (about 82 miles) of range and fast-charges from zero to 100 percent in 2 hours and 23 minutes. While most city e-bikes deliver their power modestly, Amflow is strapping a mountain-bike-grade motor onto a 20.9 kg (46 pounds) upright step-through frame — and pricing it slightly below its flagship trail bikes. The UE Carbon starts at €3,099 (about $3,500 USD), while the Pro will sell for €3,499 ($3,900 USD). [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: But this isn’t just another commuter bike. With its proprietary Avinox drivetrain, Amflow has been ahead of the curve in blending consumer gadget UX — features like wireless phone charging, Apple Watch proximity unlock, Find My integration, and camera controls — with serious hardware specs. That’s one of the reasons why The Verge’s own Thomas Ricker has been so bullish on the brand for the past few years. With 125Nm of max torque and 1,100W of peak power, the Avinox M2 in the UE Series is slightly more dialed back from Amflow’s 150Nm flagship eMTBs. That said, 125Nm is still massive overkill for flat city streets — but it won’t hurt to have it when encountering any grades over 30 percent. A new Auto Boost mode automatically dumps extra power when starting at a traffic light or hitting a steep hill. And traction control will help prevent any spin-outs on wet asphalt. The 600Wh removable battery is good for up 82 miles in Eco mode — and likely less than that while relying on higher levels of assist. It’s worth noting that the 1,100W peak power and 8x assist ratios will likely be software-capped depending on where you live and what regulations allow. [Image: As a brand within the larger DJI ecosystem, Amflow loves to integrate a lot of tech into its bikes. A 1.4 inch touchscreen is integrated into the handlebars alongside a 15W wireless phone charger — plus a 20W USB-C charger, if you prefer. The cockpit also features plenty of Apple tie-ins, like the aforementioned Find My tracker and Apple Watch proximity unlocking. The UE can also pair with a heart rate monitor, allowing riders to set a target heart rate zone that will dictate how much pedal assist the bike provides. And, of course, there’s direct recording controls for DJI Osmo cameras, in case you like to film your rides. Additional security is provided by a built-in 10mm hardened steel wheel lock keyed to match the removable battery. And if the bike is paired with “Lost Mode” in the Amflow app, the user can remotely brick the drive system if the bike ever gets stolen. There’s plenty of commuter-friendly touches, like a 65mm suspension fork, suspension dropper seatpost, and heavy-duty racks rated for 20kg (44 pounds) on the front and 27kg (60 pounds) on the rear. The bikes are on sale globally starting today via Amflow’s website and retail partners. The company says a smaller XS frame size is coming in 2027 for shorter riders. Images by Amflow

articles.title: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple's status page confirms its services are facing outages, but has not confirmed the cause.
articles.body:
After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, now it’s Apple customers who are facing technical issues.

The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates.

Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail.

On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone , which is likely related to these ongoing issues.

Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues .

Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches.

So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.

Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg ), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read.

After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com), Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program.

articles.title: JBL’s headphones that are great for in-flight entertainment are 67 percent off
articles.summary: JBL’s Tour One M3 are $149 ($300 off) ahead of Black Friday at many retailers. They come with a wireless transmitter and offer up to 70 hours of battery life.
articles.body: If you’re looking to upgrade your headphones before the big wave of Black Friday deals arrives, you can buy JBL’s Tour One M3 for a new low price of $149 ($300 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from JBL. The deal is so good that my colleague John Higgins, The Verge’s audio and TV reviewer, popped in on his day off to tell us just how much of a steal they are at this price. [Product: JBL Tour One M3 | JBL’s Tour One M3 stand out largely because they come with the Smart Tx wireless audio transmitter. Frequent fliers will likely appreciate the accessory, which plugs into a plane’s in-flight entertainment system via a 3.5mm cable, allowing you to listen to audio wirelessly. It also works with other devices that lack Bluetooth support but have a headphone jack. The small touchscreen-equipped transmitter also lets you easily adjust the headphones’ noise cancellation, EQ settings, and volume. It can be used to answer calls, too. Fancy tricks aside, the headphones get the essentials right. According to John, they offer excellent passive noise isolation, and their active noise cancellation is good enough to block out low-frequency sounds, like airplane engines. He also praises their overall sound quality, though he notes that JBL’s default tuning slightly affects midrange clarity, something you can easily fix by adjusting the EQ. They also support high-resolution lossless audio over the included USB-C or 3.5mm cable, plus spatial audio with head tracking. JBL says they can last up to 70 hours on a single charge with noise cancellation off — enough to get you through multiple long-haul flights — while the USB-C-chargeable transmitter offers up to 18 hours of battery life.

articles.title: California just banned Waymo from all state freeways
articles.summary: The California DMV has banned Waymo’s driverless robotaxis from all state freeways after recurring construction zone incursions and a CHP incident on I-280.
articles.body: California has pulled the plug on Waymo’s driverless freeway rides across the entire state, citing potential safety hazards. In a statement, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said that the ban went into effect on November 11th after two recent high-profile Bay Area incidents, in which Waymo robotaxis drove into an active construction closure on US-101 near Burlingame, and a separate run-in involving California Highway Patrol vehicles on Highway 280 in San Francisco. In its statement, the DMV explicitly labeled Waymo’s freeway operations as an “imminent hazard to public safety,” noting that this isn’t an isolated glitch. Waymo has experienced “recurring incursions into active construction zones, the DMV said, arguing the company was putting road workers at risk. Waymo has struggled with freeway operations over the years. The company has been testing its vehicles on California’s freeways since at least August 2024, before eventually opening up to public passengers in November 2025. Waymo voluntarily paused freeway operations in May 2026 over concerns about construction sites — but then resumed rides in late July. Operating on freeways is crucial to Waymo’s robotaxi business; without freeways, the company will be forced to take longer routes on local roads that will force customers to pay more for their fares. On average, Waymo rides are already more expensive than human-driven Uber or Lyft trips. In a statement, Waymo spokesperson Chris Pappas said the company voluntarily paused freeway driving across all its markets to review performance, though its surface-street ride-hailing service remains unaffected. Waymo is currently collaborating with state regulators to safely resume highway operations. “Safety is at the foundation of everything we do,” Pappas said. In order to get back on the freeway, Waymo will need to demonstrate it has taken sufficient action to improve its operation around construction zones, the DMV said. The company will need to submit evidence to the agency for review, at which point regulators will determine whether it can safely resume operations. Update, November 17th: Updated to include a statement from Waymo spokesperson.

articles.title: Framework’s better couch keyboard is now available for preorder
articles.summary: The Wireless Touchpad Keyboard uses the same hardware as some of Framework’s laptops in a slim design you can preorder today for $99.
articles.body: Framework announced its Wireless Touchpad Keyboard earlier this year with the goal of delivering a better couch keyboarding experience than the Logitech K400. According to The Verge’s Sean Hollister who went hands-on with Framework’s new all-in-one keyboard and touchpad last April, the company has succeeded in that goal, but it turns out you’ll be paying a bit more for Framework’s than Logitech’s. While the K400 couch keyboard is $35, the Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is $99 with a $50 fully refundable deposit required to preorder one starting today. That makes it nearly three times more expensive than Logitech’s, but Framework’s upgrades and improvements could make it worth the premium. [Media: Instead of starting from scratch, Framework uses the same keyboard module found in its Laptop 12 paired with a precision 120Hz touchpad and controller that’s also used in all of the company’s computers. A Bluetooth connection is the easiest way to pair the keyboard to PCs running Windows, Linux, or macOS, or mobile devices, game consoles, and streaming boxes. You can quickly switch between four wirelessly connected devices with a button press including one that uses an included USB receiver. If you want more responsiveness, you can also tether it to a device with a USB-C cable. On a full charge of its replaceable 1,200mAh battery the keyboard will run for well over a year with sporadic use. If you’re instead using it for hours every day on a desk, Framework estimates the battery life will be closer to over a month. For customizability and remapping the keyboard’s open source firmware is based on a fork of ZMK.

articles.title: Instagram is helping creators crack down on copycat videos
articles.summary: Instagram is beginning to roll out a “content protection” feature that lets creators see and review copies of their videos posted to the platform. Meta launched a similar tool for Facebook last year.
articles.body: Instagram is beginning to roll out a “content protection” feature that lets creators see and review copies of their videos posted to the platform. “For eligible creators who enroll, content protection is a tool that automatically looks out for visual matches of your original videos, alerts you when we find a match across Instagram and Facebook, and lets you decide what happens next,” Meta says in a blog post. Meta launched a similar tool for Facebook last year to help users “safeguard” their Reels and “maintain control” over their creative work. [Image: When an Instagram creator is notified of a matched video, they can see how many views the match has and decide if they want to track the video, hide it from everyone on Instagram and Facebook, add a credit link, or release their claim on the match. After a creator enrolls, every “original video” they post on Instagram is protected, and creators can retroactively protect older videos manually. Creators can also put accounts on an allow list that lets them use their videos. In addition, Instagram will start flagging AI-generated videos that “match the spoken words” in a creator’s original video but have visuals replaced with AI. Initially, Instagram will test this with a “small group of creators” in “the coming weeks.” The platform says it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of content and profiles that “use AI tools to post this type of content repeatedly.”

articles.title: Nike’s new air sole technology can mix soft and firm cushioning
articles.summary: Nike developed a new manufacturing process for its Tuned Air technology that can produce air-filled solves with varying areas of cushioning and support.
articles.body: In 2024, Nike announced its Air Max 1000 that were manufactured using a 3D-printing process resulting in a shoe that had a uniform silhouette but varying areas of support and flexibility throughout. The company is now doing something similar with its iconic air-filled soles using its new Tuned Air technology. While previously the level of cushioning in Nike Air shoes was uniform across the entire sole, a new manufacturing process can produce multiple air pockets with varying levels of cushioning and stability. Nike has been putting air pockets into its shoes for nearly 50 years as a way to increase comfort and cushioning while making them lighter. Its air pockets have even found their way into apparel as a way to improve insulation by trapping body heat, but Nike plans to use its new Tuned Air technology as a way to customize the cushioning experience in its shoes and tailor them to specific athletes and sports. The first shoes featuring the technology are expected to arrive in late 2027 and will be targeted at runners. While one of Nike’s earliest successes was track shoes with a grip design inspired by a waffle iron, the company credits the “vibrant colors on magazine covers” as the inspiration for its latest shoe technology. A Tuned Air sole is manufactured using a “proprietary digital print and selective lamination process” where an ink is applied in specific patterns that define where the layers bond to each other. This process can be used to create internal pockets in an unlimited combination of shapes and sizes, and by fine-tuning how much air is in each of those pockets, some parts of the sole can feel firmer while others feel softer. [Image: Nike’s new manufacturing process can be used to create air-filled soles with an unlimited variety of designs. The Tuned Air technology will not only allow Nike to highly customize the fit and feel of air sole shoes for different sports, it will also help keep the benefits of the custom tuning consistent across different sizes. The new manufacturing process will also help reduce the amount of time it takes Nike to go from a concept for a new shoe to a final design ready for production. “Prototypes that once took three weeks can now be made in three days,” the company claims in a release today. That gives Nike’s designers more time to refine new shoes, and more opportunity to experiment.

articles.title: The MacBook Neo is receiving a rare $50 discount ahead of Black Friday
articles.summary: Apple’s budget laptop is powered by an iPhone chip yet still delivers impressive performance for the price, with great speakers and a solid display.
articles.body: If you’re looking for a new laptop or a gift for the student in your life, you can save $50 on the MacBook Neo at several retailers, in both storage sizes and all four colors. The 256GB model is currently discounted to $649 (Amazon, Best Buy, Target), while the 512GB model with Touch ID is down to $749 (Amazon, Best Buy, Target). None of the retailers currently list an end date for the discount, which is the biggest price drop we’ve seen since Apple raised the laptop’s MSRP by $100 in July in response to the ongoing RAM crisis. [Product: MacBook Neo | Apple’s budget-friendly MacBook leverages the A18 Pro processor, a chip originally found in the iPhone 16 Pro, to keep costs down. Both the 256GB and 512GB models feature 8GB of memory, and my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto was impressed by the vivid 13-inch screen and speakers, the latter of which are better than those in many cheap (and even midrange) Windows laptops. The Neo isn’t super performant, especially in terms of storage speed and total memory, but it’s great for everyday tasks, casual use, and students. Read our Apple MacBook Neo review.

articles.title: iFixit’s Apple HomeView teardown reveals a device that will be difficult to repair
articles.summary: Although Apple has made its iPad and HomePod speakers more repairable in recent years, the HomeView is difficult to disassemble and appears to be a step back.
articles.body: After finding recent versions of Apple’s iPads and HomePods much easier to disassemble for battery replacements or other repairs, iFixit assumed it would be the same story for Apple’s new HomeView hub that looks like a seven-inch tablet stuck to a smart speaker. The reality was much different and by the time they got the HomeView apart iFixit’s skilled techs had “ripped a connector, snapped a speaker in two, and put more force on the poor logic board than any of us were comfortable with.” The tablet section of the HomeView proved to be the bigger challenge to disassemble as a result of some questionable decisions with Apple’s design. The glue used to secure the display in place “held on harder than on any Apple product we’ve opened recently,” iFixit says. And while Apple’s decision to turn the HomeView’s entire aluminum chassis into a heat sink was clever, the thermal bond between a heat shield and the device’s logic board made separating the two a “remarkably risky operation.” While these design decisions possibly streamlined assembly at a factory, the extensive use of glue makes servicing the HomeView incredibly difficult. [Media: In an accompanying teardown video iFixit also reveals how much smaller the speaker drivers are in the wall-mounted version of the HomeView versus the tabletop option. Although both versions are priced at $299, the wall version costs a little more when you factor in the required mount that’s not included, leaving iFixit feeling that you’re getting less performance while spending more money.
